questions.q: What is the essential legal requirement for a partnership firm to be dissolved by mutual agreement of all partners?
questions.a: The essential requirement is that all partners must consent to the dissolution, either expressly through a written agreement or impliedly by their conduct. A wrong answer (e.g., "majority consent is enough") reveals the misconception that partnership decisions follow majority rule like a company; in a partnership, unanimous consent is required for fundamental changes such as dissolution.

questions.q: Explain why a partner in a fixed-term partnership cannot unilaterally dissolve the firm by giving a notice under Section 43 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.
questions.a: Section 43 applies only to partnerships at will, where no fixed duration is agreed upon. In a fixed-term partnership, the partnership deed binds partners for the specified period, and unilateral notice would breach the contract. A wrong answer (e.g., "notice can be given in any partnership") shows the student has not distinguished between partnership at will and fixed-term partnership, a critical classification for determining dissolution rights.

questions.q: A partnership firm has no partnership deed. Partner A wants to retire and dissolve the firm, but Partner B wants to continue. Can Partner A dissolve the firm by giving a notice? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Yes, Partner A can dissolve the firm by giving a written notice to Partner B. In the absence of a deed, the partnership is deemed to be a partnership at will (Section 7). Under Section 43, any partner in a partnership at will may dissolve the firm by giving notice in writing to all other partners. A wrong answer (e.g., "both must agree") indicates the student assumes unanimous consent is always needed, ignoring the default rule for partnerships at will.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the grounds for dissolution by court under Section 44 with the grounds for dissolution by agreement. Why might a partner prefer court-ordered dissolution over mutual agreement?
questions.a: Dissolution by agreement requires unanimous consent of all partners and can be done for any reason. Dissolution by court (Section 44) can be sought by a partner on specific grounds such as insanity, permanent incapacity, misconduct, persistent breach of agreement, transfer of interest, or just and equitable grounds, without needing other partners' consent. A partner may prefer court dissolution when other partners refuse to agree despite serious issues like misconduct. A wrong answer that lists "disagreement on business decisions" as a court ground shows confusion between "just and equitable" (which requires a breakdown of trust, not mere disagreement) and ordinary commercial disputes.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statement: "A partnership firm can be dissolved by a partner giving notice even if the partnership deed specifies a fixed term of 5 years, provided the notice is given after 3 years." Is this statement correct? Provide legal reasoning.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. A fixed-term partnership cannot be dissolved by notice under Section 43 before the expiry of the term unless all partners agree to dissolve earlier (Section 40). The deed creates a binding contract for the fixed duration; unilateral notice would be a breach. A wrong answer that says "yes, after 3 years the notice becomes valid" reveals the misconception that the passage of time converts a fixed-term partnership into a partnership at will, which is not true unless the partnership continues beyond the term without a new agreement.

questions.q: Create a short scenario (3-4 sentences) where a partnership firm is dissolved by court order on the ground of "just and equitable" reasons, and explain why the court would grant dissolution in that scenario.
questions.a: Scenario: Partners X and Y run a manufacturing firm. Y is found to have secretly diverted firm's funds to a competing business he started, causing loss of trust. X files for dissolution. The court may grant dissolution on "just and equitable" grounds because the substratum of the partnership — mutual trust and confidence — is destroyed. A poor answer that cites "Y is not working hard" shows the student does not understand that "just and equitable" requires a fundamental breakdown, not mere dissatisfaction.
